what: The gates spike s6 (`reco-f5a`) holds its own measurement to. ADR-003 §6.2 ships three relink tiers and §13.1 defers a fourth — a fuzzy one — with the sentence 'the spike that measures the false-relink rate of the fuzzy tier decides whether it exists'. No number in this file was published before the measurement existed, which is the difference between a gate and a rubber stamp: a claim here is either a property of the shipped ladder that a future change must not break, or a floor a proposed mechanism has to clear to be worth building at all. `cargo run -p fathom-analyze --features sqlite-bundled --example s6_spike -- --check` re-measures and re-scores them.
how_gates_are_set: Passing gates are written with margin around the measured value, so that a change which makes the ladder genuinely worse trips one and a change which makes it better trips the *other* kind — a gate that starts passing has to be re-read too, which is what `expected` is for. Failing gates are the spike's findings: they are the price §6.2 and §13.1 did not know, and each one names the ticket that has to retire it. The price of a relink is stated at the rate ADR-003 §6.6 uses throughout: a wrongly-carried verdict is worse than a missing one, so a mechanism that buys carries must buy them at better than 3 carries per false relink, and the two `fuzzy-*` sparse-board gates are exactly that arithmetic.
boards: A relink can only spoil a verdict that exists, and can only be *seen* to spoil one if a human annotated where it should have gone. Two boards are therefore scored for every ladder. `signed-off` is the optimistic board: every episode in every history has been dispositioned, so every annotated carry has a verdict behind it and RL0 forbids landing on anything that already has one. `sparse` thins the review rows to every third episode, which is what a queue looks like when a third of it is still unread; on that board the same pass has more live episodes it is allowed to land on and fewer places it is forbidden. Both are reported, always, because the gap between them is one of this spike's findings and neither board alone is the truth.
scopes: pooled, or family:<name> — the rewrite families are the natural stratum here, because a relink's honesty is a property of a kind of rewrite, not of a repository.

gates.claim: the shipped §6.2 ladder loses between a quarter and 40 % of the annotated carries on the optimistic board: the hole is large and it is not made of defects

at least 350 of the carries the shipped ladder misses are ones where the annotation itself says no shipped tier had the evidence (§6.3's floor) — the misses are a limit of the digests, not a bug in the ladder
at most 30 annotated carries in the whole corpus are ones a shipped tier had the evidence for and missed anyway, which is the number §6.2's *implementation* owns, as distinct from the digests' limits

tier 1 alone (author + normalised subject) writes false relinks at a rate of at most 3 % of its rows, which is why §6.2 is right to put the exact digests first and why the digests are worth the bytes they cost

tier 2 alone (author + path set) false-relinks at 5 % or worse, four times tier 1's rate, and does it in the families where two different acts by one author touch the same set of files — a reworded `reword-batch`, a `reword-to-shared-subject`. §6.2 calls tier 2 a fallback; on this corpus it is the riskiest thing it ships
when every episode is dispositioned the shipped ladder's false relinks are at most 8 % of the rows it writes, most of them the digest-collision controls the corpus plants on purpose

the §6.3 family `reword-and-move` (message rewritten and files moved in one commit) leaves at least 150 annotated carries unreachable by any shipped tier: both digests move together, which is the case §6.3 says it cannot catch, counted
`reset-author` leaves at least 150 annotated carries unreachable: author is in every digest §6.2 computes, so an identity-preserving rewrite that changes the author is invisible to all three tiers

at least 25 annotated carries are lost to TB10 rather than to any tier: the digest survived on a twin, so the id moved and there was no dead row to relink from. This is the cost of §6.1's identity rule, not of §6.2's ladder, and it is reported separately for that reason

in the `dropped-turn` family, where the annotation says the verdict must go nowhere, the shipped ladder writes nothing at all on the optimistic board: silence is achievable and the ladder achieves it when there is nowhere to put the verdict wrong

a subject-similarity rung at 0.45, run last (RL1), buys back at least 150 of §6.3's floor carries on the optimistic board — the reason §13.1's idea is not crazy and the reason it had to be measured rather than dismissed

…and it buys those at least 150 carries for at most 50 false relinks, which is better than the 3:1 §6.6's ordering of harms requires. On a fully dispositioned queue the fuzzy tier's arithmetic works, and this gate is the whole case in its favour

buying back `reset-author`'s carries requires a rung that ignores the author (the delta between the author-agnostic and author-required rungs is at least 150 carries), i.e. the fuzzy tier's only extra prize comes from discarding the one field §6.1 says identifies the act

a pure closest-in-time rung with no window buys back at least 300 carries for at most 50 false relinks on the optimistic board — better than any similarity rung, and the most instructive number in the report: 'closest in time' is nearly free precisely because a fully dispositioned queue gives it nowhere to land wrongly
…and at most 50 false relinks while doing it, on the same board

requiring the guess to be unambiguous in both directions — one dead candidate for this live episode, and one live destination for that dead episode — holds the sparse board's price to at most 50 extra false relinks. The discipline works; that is not the problem

the shipped ladder's false relinks are at most 10 % of its rows on a queue where a third of the episodes are still unread. Measured 41 %. RL0 does not prevent a verdict being mis-stamped, it prevents it being spoiled where somebody is already looking, so every false relink lands on an episode nobody has read yet and the safety of §6.2 is a function of how far the review queue has gotten

at most 40 of the sparse board's false relinks come from one dead episode's verdict being written to more than one live episode. Measured 123 of 168: RL4 ('a dead donor may be considered by more than one live landing') plus a per-target candidate search is a multiplier, and it is invisible on a full queue only because RL0 blocks the landings

in `dropped-turn`, a verdict whose content was abandoned is written nowhere at all. Measured 19 false relinks on the sparse board: the digest collides with a stranger in the same history, the stranger has no review row yet, and RL0 is not a rule about this case. The annotation forbids the landing; the ladder's own rules do not

tier 3 (a member commit in common) buys at least 20 more carries across the corpus than the two-digest ladder alone. Measured 1. The member-set rung is decorative as written: its precondition is a commit that survives the rewrite, and a rewrite that preserves a commit is already caught by the digests. Retire this gate by giving tier 3 a predicate with reach, or by deleting the tier

the same subject rung costs at most 19 false relinks for its ≥ 150 carries on the sparse board, i.e. it still clears 3:1 where the queue looks like a queue. Measured +70 false for +57 caught: worse than one-for-one. This gate is the go/no-go §13.1 asked for, and it is the number that answers it

…and the same rung still buys at least 150 carries on a queue that looks like a queue. Measured 57: the carries it exists to buy are bought on a fully dispositioned queue and mostly vanish on a real one, because the episodes it would have to guess about are the ones with no verdict behind them. §19.2 **D1** is the decision this gate is the evidence for

the uniqueness-disciplined rung still recovers at least 150 of §6.3's 393 floor carries on the sparse board. Measured 53 — 13 % of the floor. Its *price* is fine (see `uniqueness-discipline-holds-the-price`, 6.6 carries per false relink): what is not fine is coverage, and a hand assertion through §6.4's `method='manual'` row covers all 393 at no false cost, which is the comparison §19.2 **D1** turns on

the pure recency rung's false relinks stay under 10 % of its rows on the sparse board. Measured 85 %, with 2015 of 2021 false relinks coming from a single donor landing repeatedly — the RL4 multiplier of F2 with nothing under it at all. This is what a tier with no evidence costs, and it is the counterfactual that makes the similarity rung look reasonable; it retires the day somebody proposes recency as a tie-breaker with a window

expected_semantics: Every gate declares `expected`: `pass` or `fail`. A gate that surprises us in either direction fails the contract test — a claim that starts passing has to be re-read as well as one that fails. The `fail` gates are the spike's findings, not its defects: they are the prices ADR-003 §6.2, §6.3 and §13.1 did not have, and each names the change that would retire it.
the_decision: NO-GO on the fuzzy fourth tier as §13.1 proposed it — a similarity threshold with a tuned cut-off — on `finding-fuzzy-price-on-a-real-queue` and `finding-fuzzy-carries-shrink-on-a-real-queue`: on a queue where a third of the episodes are unread it buys 0.8 carries per false relink, where §6.6's price is better than 3 carries per false relink. The uniqueness-disciplined variant is declined too, on dominance rather than price: it clears 6.6:1 but recovers 13 % of the floor, where the hand-asserted relink recovers 100 % of it at zero measured false cost. See ADR-003 §13.1 and §19.2 **D1**; `fuzzy-buys-carries-on-a-full-queue` and `fuzzy-price-on-a-full-queue` stay as the reason the idea deserved measuring.
